plan.chapterName: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 26: Biomolecules: Amino Acids, Peptides, and Proteins
plan.contextChunk: This figure pairs a titration curve for alanine with the structures present at each stage along it. The plot area is tinted pale blue and gridded; the vertical axis is labeled "pH" and runs from 0 to 12 with labeled ticks every 2 units, and the horizontal axis reads "Equivalents of HO-" and runs from 0.0 to 2.0 with ticks every 0.5. A magenta curve climbs from the bottom left in two legs, each a shallow buffering stretch followed by a steep rise, the two joined by a near-vertical jump at one equivalent. Three points on the curve are marked with an x and annotated: "pKa1 = 2.34" at 0.5 equivalent, "Isoelectric point = 6.01" at 1.0 equivalent, and "pKa2 = 9.69" at 1.5 equivalents. Thin arrows run from five positions on the curve out to bracketed structural formulas at the right, drawn with the ammonium nitrogen in magenta and the neutral amine nitrogen in blue: at the foot, the fully protonated cation with an intact carboxylic acid; at pKa1, a bracketed pair of that cation and the zwitterion; at the isoelectric point, the zwitterion alone; at pKa2, a bracketed pair of zwitterion and carboxylate anion; and at the top, the fully deprotonated anion. Aligning each structure with its own stretch of curve shows which species dominates over each pH range and pins down the pH at which the molecule carries no net charge.

interactionPlan.concept: An amino acid's titration curve maps each pH/equivalent point to a dominant protonation state, with each pKa marking a 50:50 mixture of two adjacent species and the isoelectric point (midway between the pKa values) marking the pH where the molecule exists purely as the neutral, zero-net-charge zwitterion.

interactions.label: Equivalents of HO⁻
interactions.teaches: Dragging the marker along the curve shows, at every point, the pH and which alanine protonation state dominates — cation at the foot, zwitterion in the middle, anion at the top — and that the flat buffering stretches sit at the pKa values while the steep jumps sit between them

interactions.label: Right-panel view
interactions.teaches: Switching to the net-charge view replaces each formula with its color-coded charge (+1, 0, −1), making visible that the zwitterion at pH 6.01 carries +1 and −1 simultaneously for a net charge of zero — the defining property of the isoelectric form

Clicking pKa1, the isoelectric point, or pKa2 highlights the matching curve point and its structural panel: the two pKa points each show a 50:50 bracketed pair of adjacent species (the buffering condition), whereas the isoelectric point shows a single neutral zwitterion, clarifying that pI is a pure-species point, not a mixture

demo_steps.title: Fully protonated start
demo_steps.narration: At 0 equivalents of base the curve sits at low pH and the linked structure is the fully protonated cation (magenta H3N⁺ and intact COOH), carrying a net +1 charge.

demo_steps.title: First buffering region (pKa1)
demo_steps.narration: At 0.5 equivalents the marker rests on the flat leg at pH 2.34; the right panel shows a 50:50 bracketed pair of cation and zwitterion — the hallmark of a pKa, where two adjacent species coexist equally.

demo_steps.title: Isoelectric point
demo_steps.narration: At 1.0 equivalent the curve jumps steeply through pH 6.01 and the linked structure is the zwitterion alone; in net-charge view its +1 and −1 cancel to zero, showing why this is the isoelectric (no-net-charge) form.

demo_steps.title: Second buffering region (pKa2)
demo_steps.narration: At 1.5 equivalents the marker sits on the upper flat leg at pH 9.69, where the zwitterion and the fully deprotonated anion (blue H2N) coexist 50:50; beyond 2.0 equivalents only the net −1 anion remains.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Each pKa is a 50:50 mixture of two adjacent protonation states (the flat buffering legs), while the isoelectric point — exactly between the two pKa values — is the single pH where alanine exists purely as the neutral zwitterion with zero net charge.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Left two-thirds is the plot: pale-blue tinted rectangle with light gray gridlines, magenta S-shaped two-leg titration curve rising from bottom-left to top-right with a near-vertical step at x=1.0. Three black 'x' markers with curved leader arrows to italic labels 'pKa1 = 2.34', 'Isoelectric point = 6.01', 'pKa2 = 9.69'. Right third holds five bracketed structural formulas stacked vertically, each connected by a thin straight arrow to its matching height on the curve: bottom = cation (H3N⁺ magenta, COOH magenta), then [cation + zwitterion], middle = zwitterion alone (H3N⁺ magenta, COO⁻), then [zwitterion + anion], top = anion (H2N blue, COO⁻). Keep ammonium N magenta and neutral amine N blue consistently. A filled marker dot rides the curve at the slider position with a small pH readout; the currently dominant right-hand structure gets a highlight outline. In net-charge view, swap each formula for a colored charge badge (+1 magenta, 0 gray/green, −1 blue) so the zwitterion's cancellation to zero is obvious.

authoredContext:
Solving the two simultaneous equations gives [HA] = 0.83 and [A–] = 0.17. In other words, at pH = 9.00, 83% of alanine molecules in a 1.00 M solution are neutral (zwitterionic) and 17% are deprotonated. Similar calculations can be done at other pH values and the results plotted to give the titration curve shown in the figure.

Look carefully at the titration curve in the figure. In acid solution, the amino acid is protonated and exists primarily as a cation. In basic solution, the amino acid is deprotonated and exists primarily as an anion. In between the two is an intermediate pH at which the amino acid is exactly balanced between anionic and cationic forms, existing primarily as the neutral, dipolar zwitterion. This pH is called the amino acid’s isoelectric point (pI) and has a value of 6.01 for alanine.

Each leg of the titration curve is calculated separately. The first leg, from pH 1 to 6, corresponds to the dissociation of protonated alanine, H2A+. The second leg, from pH 6 to 11, corresponds to the dissociation of zwitterionic alanine, HA. It’s as if we started with H2A+ at low pH and then titrated with NaOH. When 0.5 equivalent of NaOH is added, the deprotonation of H2A+ is 50% complete; when 1.0 equivalent of NaOH is added, the deprotonation of H2A+ is finished and HA predominates; when 1.5 equivalents of NaOH is added, the deprotonation of HA is 50% complete; and when 2.0 equivalents of NaOH is added, the deprotonation of HA is finished.

A titration curve for alanine, plotted using the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation. Each of the two legs is plotted separately. At pH < 1, alanine is entirely protonated; at pH = 2.34, alanine is a 50: 50 mix of protonated and neutral forms; at pH = 6.01, alanine is entirely neutral; at pH = 9.69, alanine is a 50: 50 mix of neutral and deprotonated forms; at pH > 11.5, alanine is entirely deprotonated.

The figure shows the titration curve for alanine. The x-axis represents equivalents of hydroxide ion and the y-axis represents the pH. It shows isoelectric point and two dissociation constant values.

discrepancies: The structural formulas on the right are rendered as small text-based approximations (separate text elements for each atom/group connected by simple lines) rather than the cleaner, larger chemical structure drawings in the source
The carboxyl group is split into separate 'C' and 'OH'/'O⁻' text elements with a tiny bond line between them, whereas the source renders 'COOH'/'CO⁻' as a more visually connected unit
The right-side structures appear noticeably smaller relative to the plot area compared to the source, making them harder to read at inline size
evaluation.notes: The titration curve, axis ranges, gridlines, X markers, pKa/pI labels with curved arrows, and species-to-curve connecting arrows are all faithfully reproduced with correct chemistry; the main weakness is that the structural formulas are rendered as small text-based approximations that are harder to read than the source's clean drawings, though all species, colors, and charge states are correct.
action_items: Increase the font size and bond line lengths in drawSpecies() so the structural formulas are more legible at inline rendering size (e.g. fs=16 instead of 12, proportionally longer bonds)
Render the carboxyl group as a single text element 'COOH' or 'CO⁻' rather than splitting into 'C' + 'OH'/'O⁻' with a tiny connecting line, to better match the source's visual style
Consider increasing the overall scale factor of the right-side structure panel or reducing the plot area width to give structures more horizontal space
